content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the same core: sapphire symbolizes heaven, divine glory, and above all the throne/manifest presence of God, anchored in Exodus 24:10, Ezekiel 1:26, and Ezekiel 10:1, with Revelation 21:19 as eschatological reinforcement. Secondary meanings (purity, contemplation, God's people as jewels, wisdom's worth, tribal/apostolic mappings) are treated as elaborations, and the lapis-lazuli identification is a lexical footnote. No response mentions any lunar association.","book_summary":"The book identifies sapphire as the full moon in its enthroned and bridal form — the clear sapphire likeness seen at the place of God's throne. Its 'clearness' (tohar, Ex 24:10) is linked to a throne-glory that can be made to cease (Ps 89:44), i.e., a reflected, borrowed brightness ('worn, not owned'), and the stone is assigned to the tribe of Issachar. The book's own common-view note concedes the standard reading is 'the blue of heaven itself... no lunar identification.'","consensus_core_identification":"Sapphire = the heavenly realm and the throne/glory of God (theophanic blue of heaven).","book_core_identification":"Sapphire = the full moon as bride and throne-likeness, a derivative and revocable brightness reflecting the throne-glory; tribally assigned to Issachar.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains the throne-vision passages (Ex 24:10; Ezek 1:26; 10:1; Rev 21:19) but reclassifies what the sapphire in them denotes: not heaven/God's own glory directly, but the moon as a bridal, dependent bearer of that glory. It adds lunar and bridal texts the consensus never invokes (Ps 89:36-37, 44; Song 6:9-10; Job 37:18, 21; Isa 54:5) and injects a mutable/cessation dimension ('made to cease,' Lam 4:7-8 darkening) absent from all consensus readings.","material_contradiction":"The consensus reads the sapphire as the blue of heaven itself and the immediate splendor of God's throne — an intrinsic, transcendent glory. The book explicitly denies this ('no lunar identification' is flagged as the common view it departs from) and substitutes the moon: a created luminary whose brightness is reflected, bridal, and capable of being made to cease (Ps 89:44). A glory that is God's own transcendent presence and a glory that is 'worn, not owned' and revocable cannot both be the sapphire's referent in the same sense; accepting the lunar-bridal identification requires replacing the consensus identification, not merely refining it.","rationale":"Both readings occupy the same scriptural sites (the throne visions), but the central referent differs: consensus = heaven/God's throne-glory itself; book = the full moon as enthroned bride reflecting that glory. The book's own common-view note confirms it knows and rejects the consensus referent. No consensus response or listed alternative anticipates a lunar, bridal, or mutable-glory reading, nor the Issachar assignment as a settled claim. Because the book replaces the identification rather than narrowing its boundary, this is DIVERGENT rather than REFINED, and because the consensus baseline exists and is contradicted, it is not NOVEL.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book merely refines rather than replaces: the moon-as-throne reading still keeps sapphire tied to the throne and heavenly glory (the consensus category), only specifying which celestial body embodies it. The printed citations give the chain some traction — Ps 89:36-37 pairs the throne with the moon as 'a faithful witness in heaven,' Ps 89:44 speaks of throne-glory made to cease, Song 6:10 gives a bridal figure 'fair as the moon,' and Lam 4:7-8 shows sapphire brightness turning black. But no verse identifies sapphire with the moon; the argument is a multi-step inference across unlinked texts, and the book itself frames the lunar identification as contrary to what is 'commonly taught,' which supports DIVERGENT over REFINED.","confidence":"high"}
